newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin on fighting form before Clinton summit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin on fighting form before Clinton summit.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin showed fighting form on Monday for this week's summit with Bill Clinton, lashing out at Washington's policies and teasing the U.S. president over his recent fall.

With an eye to his domestic critics, Yeltsin raised the spectre of a return to the Cold War, saying U.S.-Russian relations had to be equal and Russian diplomats could offer no more concessions to their U.S. counterparts.

On a lighter note and with evident relish at his own recovery from months of heart problems, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader said he had foiled predictions that he would be the sick man at the summit in the Finnish capital Helsinki.

"They said that a sick Yeltsin and a healthy Clinton would come to Helsinki and it turns out the other way around," Yeltsin said in an interview with Russian, American and Finnish television reporters.

Yeltsin is under strong pressure from nationalist and communist foes not to be seen to take a soft line with Clinton over NATO's plans to expand eastwards -- a topic which is expected to dominate the summit starting on Thursday.
"I don't want a return to the Cold War, I don't want it and our people don't want it, but for that there must be equal conditions in the world order," he said.
Yeltsin said that Russia, which argues that NATO expansion threatens its security, was not worried about a possible attack, but about economic and strategic isolation.
"I'm not worried that NATO will attack, Russia would simply hit back," said Yeltsin. "What I am afraid of is that blockade, a blockade of Russia by the West which we cannot allow."
"How we can accept a military organisation activating around our borders and openly at that?" he added in answer to a question by U.S. network NBC (National Broadcasting Company).
"Why, against Russia's wishes, are they preparing to have (military) excerises in the Crimea, in the Black Sea?" he said.
Russia has refused to join the excercises, scheduled to be hosted in August by neighbouring Ukraine under the auspices of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme deepening military ties.
The United States, Britain, Germany and France are among countries due to take part in the wargames, seen by Moscow as a provocative move right on its doorstep.

The Russian president extended his tough talk in the interview to economic issues too, in a futher sign Moscow hopes to use the NATO issue to extract economic concessions from the United States and the international community as a whole.

"Why, up to now, can Russia not join various world organisations because of U.S. opposition? Why is Russia not recognised as having a market economy yet? Why? Seventy percent is in the private sector," Yeltsin protested.

Complaining that other countries with much smaller economies had invested more than the United States in Russia since the collapse of communist rule in 1991, Yeltsin reiterated that the summit would be tough.
"There has not been such a difficult meeting as this between me and an American president, (George) Bush or Bill Clinton."
When plans for the summit began being laid last year, the trickiest issue appeared to be Yeltsin's health after the Russian leader underwent heart bypass surgery in November.

"Yes, I really was ill, but so what? You see no one is insured against illness. Bill Clinton suddenly also got sick," said Yeltsin, whose ill health was the reason the summit is to be held in the capital of Russia's northern neighbour.
"I am in good form today, today I am able, so to say, to rule the state and in fact I am in better form today than before the illness," he said.
